title: WHY DOES THE HOLY SPIRIT KEEP POINTING YOU TO JESUS?
paragraphs: WHY DOES THE HOLY SPIRIT KEEP POINTING YOU TO JESUS?
If the Spirit of God truly lives in you, He will never make Himself the destination. He will keep turning your eyes toward the One your soul cannot survive without.
There is something almost unsettling about the way the Holy Spirit works.
He can convict you until the secret thing you have hidden for years suddenly feels unbearable.
He can comfort you when nobody knows you cried yourself to sleep.
He can interrupt a perfectly ordinary morning with a Scripture you have read a hundred times—and somehow, on that particular day, it reads you.
He can expose pride without destroying you.
He can uncover sin without abandoning you.
He can bring memories to the surface you thought you had buried.
He can make Jesus feel more precious than the thing you were once terrified to surrender.
But here is what is remarkable.
The Holy Spirit does not do any of this so that your attention ultimately terminates on the Holy Spirit.
He points you to Jesus.
Again.
And again.
And again.
And if you have ever wondered why, the answer takes us directly into the heart of the Trinity, the mission of Christ, and the reason God refuses to leave sinners trapped inside their own stories.
Jesus told His disciples exactly what the Spirit would do.
Speaking about the coming Holy Spirit, Christ said:
“Ἐκεῖνος ἐμὲ δοξάσει.”
“ἐκεῖνος” — He.
“ἐμὲ” — Me.
“δοξάσει” — will glorify.
“He will glorify Me.”
Those words come from John 16:14.
Read them slowly.
Jesus did not say that the Spirit would come primarily to make Christians fascinated with spiritual experiences.
He did not say the Spirit would come so believers could become obsessed with manifestations, personalities, platforms, emotional sensations, or themselves.
Jesus said:
“He will glorify Me.”
That is the direction of the Spirit’s ministry.
Toward Christ.

This does not diminish the Holy Spirit. It reveals the beautiful harmony of the Triune God. The Father sends the Son. The Son accomplishes redemption. The Spirit applies Christ’s work, bears witness to Christ, opens hearts to Christ, transforms believers into Christ’s likeness, and glorifies Christ.
There is no competition within God.
The Father loves the Son.
The Son glorifies the Father.
The Spirit glorifies the Son.
And sinners are brought into the breathtaking reality of God’s redeeming love.
That means one of the clearest questions you can ask about anything claiming to be “spiritual” is painfully simple:
Where is it taking me?
Closer to Jesus?
Or closer to myself?
Because not everything spiritual is the Holy Spirit.
And not everything emotional is revival.
Not everything supernatural is from God.
Not every voice saying “God told me” has actually heard from God.
The Holy Spirit has fingerprints.
And one of the unmistakable fingerprints of His work is that Jesus Christ becomes increasingly magnificent.
Jesus said in John 15:26:
“When the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, He will bear witness about Me.”
The Greek expression is:
“μαρτυρήσει περὶ ἐμοῦ”
“He will bear witness concerning Me.”
There it is again.
Jesus.
The Spirit bears witness to Christ.
Why?
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of human beings becoming better versions of themselves.
It is the story of dead sinners being reconciled to God through the crucified and risen Son.
And that changes everything.
Maybe you have spent years thinking Christianity was mostly about becoming respectable.
Stop swearing.
Stop drinking too much.
Go to church.
Read your Bible.
Pray more.
Be nicer.
Try harder.
Do better.
And certainly, genuine faith produces obedience. Jesus transforms behavior.
But Christianity begins much deeper than behavior modification.
The Gospel confronts something far more devastating.
We do not merely do sinful things.
We are sinners who need reconciliation with a holy God.
We cannot save ourselves.
We cannot perform our way into righteousness.
We cannot scrub the stains from our own souls.
We cannot negotiate with death.
We cannot climb high enough to reach God.
So God came down to us.
Jesus Christ entered our world.
The eternal Son took on human flesh.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
And there, the innocent One suffered for the guilty.
The sinless One bore sin.
The righteous One died for the unrighteous.
Isaiah had spoken centuries earlier of the suffering Servant:
“וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ”
“He was pierced because of our transgressions.”
Isaiah 53:5.
Not because He had sinned.
Because we had.
The cross is scandalous precisely because grace is scandalous.
The guilty walk free because the Innocent One took their place.
The ashamed are covered.
The condemned are pardoned.
The wandering are called home.
The spiritually dead are made alive.
And then came Sunday.
The tomb did not keep Him.
Jesus rose.
Christianity does not proclaim merely the teachings of a dead religious teacher.
We proclaim a risen King.
And this is why the Holy Spirit keeps bringing you back to Jesus.
Because Jesus is not an accessory to Christianity.
Jesus is Christianity’s center.
Take Christ away and there is no Gospel left.
This is also why conviction can hurt so deeply.
Have you ever been sitting quietly and suddenly remembered something you did years ago?
Something nobody knows.
Something you wish you could erase.
Maybe everyone thinks you are doing well.
You smile.
You work.
You post.
You laugh.
You attend church.
You tell people, “I’m okay.”
But somewhere underneath all of it is a room in your soul you keep locked.
A relationship.
An addiction.
A betrayal.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Pride.
A secret conversation.
An unforgiven wound.
A double life.
A compromise you renamed so you would not have to call it sin.
And then Scripture gets through the door.
Suddenly the excuses stop working.
That can feel terrifying.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
The Spirit exposes sin so that sinners will run toward the Savior.
He does not reveal the wound merely to make you stare at the wound.
He points you toward the Physician.
He does not reveal chains merely to make you ashamed of your chains.
He points you toward the Deliverer.
He does not show you your guilt and whisper, “Now hide from God.”
He shows you your need and points toward the blood of Jesus.
This is why biblical conviction and hopeless despair move in different directions.
Despair says:
“You are filthy. Hide.”
The Gospel says:
“You have sinned. Come to Christ.”
Shame says:
“If people knew, you would be finished.”
Grace says:
“Jesus already knows—and He still calls sinners to repent and come.”
Pride says:
“Fix yourself first.”
Jesus says:
“Come.”
And maybe that is exactly where this article found you.
Not when everything is going beautifully.
But when something inside you is tired.
You have been fighting the same temptation.
Making the same promise.
Returning to the same secret.
Asking forgiveness for something you swore you would never do again.
Maybe you have even wondered whether God has finally become tired of you.
Listen carefully.
Grace is not permission to keep embracing sin.
Grace is the reason you no longer have to remain enslaved to it.
The Holy Spirit does not comfort us into comfortable rebellion.
He leads us into truth.
Jesus said in John 16:13:
“ὁδηγήσει ὑμᾶς ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ πάσῃ”
“He will guide you into all the truth.”
Truth sometimes comforts.
Truth sometimes cuts.
Truth sometimes tells you that the relationship you keep defending is destroying you.
Truth sometimes tells you that what culture celebrates God calls sin.
Truth sometimes tells you your anger is becoming hatred.
Truth sometimes tells you your religious performance has become pride.
Truth sometimes tells you that the person you blame for everything is not responsible for everything happening inside your heart.
And truth sometimes tells you something equally difficult to believe:
You are not beyond the reach of Christ’s mercy.
That may be the truth some people resist most.
We can become strangely attached to our shame.
We punish ourselves because punishment feels more reasonable than forgiveness.
We replay the failure.
We revisit the scene.
We imagine what we should have done.
We quietly sentence ourselves again every morning.
But self-condemnation cannot pay for sin.
Jesus already went to the cross.
You do not honor His sacrifice by pretending your sin was insignificant.
But neither do you honor His sacrifice by acting as though His blood is insufficient.
Repentance looks honestly at sin and then looks desperately to Christ.
And the Holy Spirit keeps turning your face in that direction.
Jesus.
When you fall—Jesus.
When you are tempted—Jesus.
When success makes you proud—Jesus.
When grief makes you numb—Jesus.
When people applaud you—Jesus.
When people abandon you—Jesus.
When you cannot understand what God is doing—Jesus.
When death finally comes knocking—Jesus.
Not because His name is a religious slogan.
Because He is Lord.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 12:3:
“No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except by the Holy Spirit.”
This means the Spirit does not merely make Jesus interesting.
He opens our understanding to Christ’s lordship.
Jesus is not merely a life coach.
Not merely a moral philosopher.
Not merely someone who helps you achieve your dreams.
Not merely someone added to an otherwise self-directed life.
Κύριος Ἰησοῦς.
Jesus is Lord.
And that is where modern Christianity can become uncomfortable.
Because everyone wants a Savior when drowning.
Far fewer want a Lord when deciding how to live.
We want Jesus to forgive the sin while leaving the throne untouched.
We want salvation without surrender.
Comfort without correction.
Heaven without holiness.
Grace without repentance.
A cross that decorates the wall but never crucifies our pride.
But the Holy Spirit loves us too much to build our lives around a counterfeit Jesus.
He reveals the real Christ.
Holy.
Merciful.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
Coming again.
The Jesus who forgives adulterers and tells them to leave sin.
The Jesus who welcomes broken people and confronts religious hypocrites.
The Jesus who touches lepers and overturns tables.
The Jesus who weeps at graves and commands dead men to come out.
The Jesus who receives sinners but refuses to pretend sin does not matter.
The Jesus whose grace is free to us precisely because it cost Him so much.
And something begins happening when the Spirit turns our eyes toward this Jesus.
We change.
Not overnight perfection.
Not performative Christianity.
Transformation.

Paul describes it in 2 Corinthians 3:18. As believers behold the Lord’s glory, they are being transformed—“μεταμορφούμεθα,” being changed—into the same image from glory to glory, and Paul says this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.
Notice the pattern.
Beholding.
Then becoming.
We become increasingly like the One we keep looking at.
That may explain why the enemy fights so relentlessly for your attention.
Keep staring at comparison.
Keep staring at outrage.
Keep staring at pornography.
Keep staring at yourself.
Keep staring at your failures.
Keep staring at other people’s lives.
Keep staring at everything except Christ.
Because whatever continually captures your gaze eventually begins shaping your heart.
But the Spirit keeps whispering through Scripture:
Look again.
Look at Jesus.
Look at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Look at the mercy you did not earn.
Look at the King who was willing to wear thorns.
Look at the hands pierced for sinners.
Look at the Savior who knew the worst chapter before He ever called your name.
And suddenly your scandal does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
That is the heartbeat behind Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal is imaginary.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus Christ can write redemption into places sin tried to turn into endings.
Peter denied Him.
Three times.
Imagine carrying that memory.
“I do not know the man.”
Then the rooster.
Then the eyes of Jesus.
Then bitter weeping.
If Peter’s story ended there, he would forever be remembered as the disciple who failed when courage mattered most.
But Jesus was not finished writing.
After the resurrection, Christ restored Peter.
The mouth that denied Jesus would eventually proclaim Jesus.
The frightened disciple became a witness.
Failure was real.
Grace was greater.
That is not permission to sin.
That is hope for sinners who repent.
Maybe you need that hope today.
Maybe your worst chapter has become your identity.
Divorced.
Addicted.
Unfaithful.
Rejected.
Lukewarm.
Angry.
Compromised.
Broken.
Hypocrite.
Failure.
What if Jesus has another word?
Forgiven.
Redeemed.
Restored.
Mine.
Not automatically.
Not because everyone eventually gets a happy ending regardless of Christ.
But because everyone who truly turns to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith discovers that the cross is strong enough to carry what they cannot.
The Holy Spirit points people to Jesus because there is no greater destination for a sinner.
He points to Jesus because Christ reveals the Father.
He points to Jesus because Christ accomplished redemption.
He points to Jesus because Christ defeated death.
He points to Jesus because Christ is our righteousness, our hope, our King.
And He points to Jesus because the Christian life cannot be lived by staring endlessly at ourselves.
Perhaps the most spiritual thing you can do tonight is not chase another experience.
Maybe it is simply to become honest before God.
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, I have been pretending.”
“Jesus, I have been blaming everyone else.”
“Jesus, I have been trying to save myself.”
“Jesus, I need mercy.”
There is no magic in repeating words.
But there is salvation in Christ.
Turn to Him.
Confess your sin.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
And when you fall, do not build a house on the ground.
Get up and run toward Christ again.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you can stop pretending.
Someone reading silently may need evidence that Jesus still restores broken lives.
Then think of one person who needs this truth.
Not fifty random people.
One.
The friend quietly drifting from God.
The son who stopped going to church.
The woman carrying shame from her past.
The husband who has become spiritually numb.
The believer who keeps falling and thinks Jesus is finished with him.
The unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is only about religious people pretending to be good.
Sharing cannot save them.
Jesus can.
But perhaps your share becomes the doorway through which they encounter His Word.

There may come a night when shame becomes loud again, when temptation feels stronger than conviction, or when you simply need to remember why the Holy Spirit keeps turning your eyes back toward Jesus.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
And please remember this before you leave.
Your support may help carry the message.
Your share may put the Gospel in front of someone who desperately needs it.
Your comment may remind another wounded believer that they are not fighting alone.
But Jesus is still the Savior.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not a preacher.
Not a church brand.
Not an emotional experience.
Jesus.
That is exactly why the Holy Spirit keeps pointing people back to Him.

Because when the noise disappears, when platforms disappear, when applause disappears, when possessions disappear, when our carefully constructed identities disappear, and when every human heart finally stands before eternity, there will be only one name upon which sinners can place their hope.
Jesus Christ.
So when the Spirit convicts you, do not run from Jesus.
When the Spirit exposes you, do not hide from Jesus.
When the Spirit reminds you of Scripture, listen.
When the Spirit reveals your pride, repent.
When the Spirit exposes your wounds, bring them into the light.
When the Spirit makes Christ beautiful to you again, look.
Keep looking.
Because perhaps the greatest evidence that God is rewriting your story is not that you have finally become impressed with yourself.
It is that you are becoming increasingly captivated by Jesus.
And perhaps your story has chapters you would burn if you could.
Christ already knows every page.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
Bring Him the heart you cannot repair.
Then watch what grace does when a surrendered sinner places the pen back into the hands of Jesus.
Your darkest chapter does not have to become your final sentence when Jesus Christ is still writing.
